plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic three-dimensional depiction of a hydrogen atom drawn as one large sphere. The sphere is rendered as a grey outline circle with a paler grey ellipse across its middle standing for an equatorial plane, which gives the drawing depth. At the center sits a small dark blue disc bearing a plus sign, representing the proton. A second, much smaller pale blue sphere representing the electron is placed on the upper right of the spherical surface, and a thin blue arc curves down to it from the top of the sphere. A straight black line labeled r joins the central charge to the electron, and a thick red arrow labeled F lies along that same line, pointing from the electron back toward the nucleus. A vertical dashed line through the center, a horizontal dashed line across the equatorial ellipse, and faint blue dashed guides dropping from the electron to that ellipse fix the electron's position in three dimensions. Drawing the force antiparallel to r conveys at a glance that the interaction is attractive and directed along the line joining the two particles. The sketch sets up a Coulomb's law calculation of the force on the ground-state electron at its most probable distance from the proton.

elements: central proton at the origin (dark blue sphere with a white '+' sign)
dashed X, Y, and Z axes intersecting at the origin
reference spherical shell (represented by a grey equatorial ring and a vertical polar axis)
radius vector r (straight black line from proton to electron)
force vector F (red arrow starting at the electron and pointing toward the proton)
meridian arc (solid blue curve along the sphere surface from the north pole down to the electron)
dashed projection drop lines connecting the electron to the equatorial plane, and from there to the axes
labels: 'r' near the black line, 'F' near the red arrow

interactions.teaches: The 3D spatial arrangement of the particles and the alignment of the force vector along the radial line.
Moving the electron anywhere on the sphere demonstrates that the attractive Coulomb force always points strictly radially inward, forming a central force field.

interactions.label: Separation r
interactions.teaches: Changing the distance reveals the inverse-square nature of Coulomb's law; as r increases, the force arrow shrinks rapidly.

demo_steps.title: Central Force Direction
demo_steps.narration: The force F on the electron is attractive, always pointing strictly radially inward along the line connecting it to the proton. Drag the electron to see this holds everywhere.

demo_steps.title: Inverse-Square Magnitude
demo_steps.narration: Increase the separation r. The red force arrow shrinks rapidly, reflecting the 1/r² dependence of the Coulomb force. At r=2, it is one-quarter its original length.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Proton: Sphere ~0.15 units radius at origin, dark blue #1f4e79 with a '+' texture. Electron: Sphere ~0.08 units radius, pale blue #5b9bd5. Fixed dashed axes span ±2.5 units to provide a stable scale. The grey equatorial ring and meridian arc scale dynamically so their radius always equals the slider value 'r'. The red force arrow (#c00000) length scales as 0.2 / r², starting from the electron and pointing at the origin. Dragging updates the electron's polar and azimuthal angles without changing r. Drop lines: dashed lines from (x, y, z) down to (x, 0, z), then connecting to the X and Z axes.
interactionPlan.notes: Map the drag interaction to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) mapped onto the current radius r. Update the red arrow's length and orientation reactively on both drag and slider change. The equator should be a simple LineLoop in the XZ plane (assuming Y is up) to match standard 3D spherical coordinate geometry.

authoredContext:
The Force on the Electron in Hydrogen A hydrogen atom consists of a single proton and a single electron. The proton has a charge of +e and the electron has −e. In the “ground state” of the atom, the electron orbits the proton at most probable distance of 5.29×10−11m (the figure). Calculate the electric force on the electron due to the proton.

A schematic depiction of a hydrogen atom, showing the force on the electron. This depiction is only to enable us to calculate the force; the hydrogen atom does not really look like this. Recall another section.

A positive charge is shown at the center of a sphere of radius r. An electron is depicted as a particle on the sphere. The force on the electron is along the radius, toward the nucleus.

Strategy For the purposes of this example, we are treating the electron and proton as two point particles, each with an electric charge, and we are told the distance between them; we are asked to calculate the force on the electron. We thus use Coulomb’s law.

discrepancies: The coordinate axes extend symmetrically in both positive and negative directions, adding visual clutter, whereas the original axes originate from the center.
The coordinate axes extend significantly beyond the outer spherical shell, whereas the original axes end near the shell boundary.
The central proton is rendered with a somewhat blurry canvas texture and drawn rectangles for the plus sign, rather than a crisp graphic or text symbol.
The electron uses a flat BasicMaterial, missing the subtle specular highlight and shading seen in the original.
evaluation.notes: An excellent interactive figure that perfectly captures the physics concept with a clever dragging implementation, though the visual presentation is slightly cluttered by overly long, bidirectional axes.
action_items: Modify the coordinate axes to start at the origin (0,0,0) and extend only in the positive directions to match the reference.
Shorten the coordinate axes so they do not extend significantly past the outer spherical shell.
Change the electron's material to MeshStandardMaterial or MeshPhongMaterial with a directional light to provide a specular highlight.
Improve the central proton's resolution by using a higher-resolution canvas, or replace it with a 3D sphere combined with a floating HTML label for a crisp '+' sign.
